title: Greedy Best-First on New York (SoHo) ⚡
description: Visualizing Greedy Best-First pathfinding on New York (SoHo)
ig_caption:
Greedy Best-First Search vs A*: Pathfinding Comparison — why it rushes to the goal ⚡

In this Barcelona (Eixample) visualization, Greedy Best-First expands the next node with the lowest heuristic h(n) (think: “distance-to-go” from the grid). It does NOT balance real travel cost g(n), so it can look optimal while ignoring costly detours.

What you’ll notice on screen:
• It feels lightning-fast because it’s guided only by heuristic path distance.
• It can fail in “greedy traps” (local minima / misleading heuristics), where the closest-looking route leads into dead ends or long detours.
• Contrast with A*: A* combines g(n)+h(n), which reduces these traps and improves reliability for shortest paths.

Takeaway: If your heuristic is accurate and obstacles don’t bait you, greedy can be quick. If the heuristic lies, Greedy Best-First can confidently choose the wrong hallway.

Debate question: Should pathfinding prioritize “fast arrival” (greedy) or “guaranteed best route” (A*)?

Greedy Best-First Search vs A*: Pathfinding Comparison (Barcelona Eixample) — why Greedy Best-First rushes toward destinations and when it fails ⚡

In this Short Video, we visualize heuristic pathfinding with Greedy Best-First: it chooses the next node using only h(n) (distance-to-go), ignoring g(n) cost-so-far. You’ll see greedy best first search win on open routes—and get trapped when the heuristic points toward a dead end.

Compare with A* (f(n)=g(n)+h(n)) and understand greedy vs a star in real map routing.
